features.name: Form-encoded project writes silently set is_active=False
features.description: ProjectSerializer exposes is_active, and DRF sets BooleanField.default_empty_html = False, so for multipart/form bodies a missing boolean is read as False rather than as 'not supplied'. A POST without is_active therefore creates a project that get_queryset() hides from the default list, and a PUT deactivates an existing one; the identical body sent as JSON keeps is_active=True. Pinned by test_create_via_form_data_lands_inactive and test_put_without_is_active_deactivates_project. The same trap applies to any serializer exposing a BooleanField whose model default is True.

features.name: Project restore response nests the project under a 'topic' key

features.name: Unordered querysets paginated in template_form and working_form

features.name: AI-assisted scoring
features.description: Considered and REJECTED 2026-09-02 during the ideation for AI-7 and AI-8. Kept rather than deleted, because a registry that retains only the winning options starts lying within a year about whether alternatives were ever weighed. The original shape - AI proposes a score plus a rationale from the interviewer's notes or the transcript, and the interviewer confirms it before submitting - is recorded in docs/features/ai-answer-scoring-from-transcript/idea-brief.md section 14 as a parked-and-rejected approach. The reason is anchoring: a suggested score visible before the interviewer has committed destroys the independence of the second opinion, and that independence is the entire downstream product value, because AI-8 exists to compare two judgements formed apart. Confirm-style assistance also cannot be undone once shipped - an interviewer who has seen a proposed number cannot un-see it, so there is no A/B to recover from. The accepted alternative scores independently and stays hidden until the interviewer's own feedback is submitted; the existing submitted-feedback lock already provides the natural boundary for that reveal, so no new gate is needed. This entry stays open rather than closed because a confirm-style assist may still be correct where no divergence signal is wanted downstream - drafting questions for the bank is the obvious candidate - but it must not sit on the interview-scoring path.

features.name: Note-taker integration with independent AI answer scoring
features.description: Interview transcript from a note-taker (Recall.ai / Fireflies) mapped to form questions; AI independently scores each candidate answer on the same 0-3 scale. Brief: docs/features/ai-answer-scoring-from-transcript/idea-brief.md, status Confirmed 2026-09-02, RICE 7.0, feasibility 2 of 3, decision 'Approach C - Post-Submit Calibration Loop'. Deliberately NOT merged with AI-8: the brief's frontmatter cites the pair 'AI-7 + AI-8' as its ticket, so collapsing the two ids would break a citation that points here. AI-7 is the producer of the paired score, AI-8 the consumer; AI-7 is a hard prerequisite and nothing in AI-8 can be built or validated before it ships. The rejected alternative shape for this scoring is recorded under AI-2.

features.name: Divergence report (AI vs interviewer scores)
features.description: Per-question comparison of AI and interviewer scores with rationale; used for interview quality control and interviewer calibration. Brief: docs/features/divergence-report/idea-brief.md, status Confirmed 2026-09-02, RICE 9.0 computed at the measured floor of 45 disputed candidates per quarter (ceiling 120), feasibility 0 of 3 - blocked on AI-7, which does not exist in code. Decision: none of the three proposed approaches survived intact; the accepted shape is a hybrid assembled from all three - the containment of the cheapest one (no machine scores means an empty screen, not a broken one), the survival rule of the most invasive one stated as narrowly as it can be, an explicit marker so that 'not comparable' can never look like 'no divergence', and the interview-moment anchor of the most expensive one, without which three separate review lenses agreed the metric cannot move. One correction outranks all of them and is recorded here because it changes what gets built: the report is produced for EVERY completed evaluation, not only before a rejection. Building it only on the losing side makes the scorer unvalidatable - there is no comparison group, every retained report belongs to a rejected candidate - and it has the shape of selective application of an assessment instrument to the people being turned down. Residual risk, tracked as an open question in the brief: reading will still concentrate on rejections, so read frequency must be measured separately from build frequency, otherwise the one-sidedness returns through behaviour after being designed out of the construction.

features.name: HR analytics
features.description: Interviewer load and consistency, hiring quality tracking, panel diversity, dashboards for hiring managers. Relationship to AI-8 clarified 2026-09-02: it is supplier-to-consumer, not duplication. AI-8 produces the per-question divergence between a human score and a machine score for one candidate, plus the calibration profile that accumulates those divergences per interviewer; this entry aggregates them across interviews and renders them. Neither entry should absorb the other - the consistency signal here is worthless without the pairing AI-8 defines, and the pairing is worthless to a hiring manager without the aggregation here. One caution carried over from the AI-8 devil's-advocate pass and worth reading before any dashboard is designed: 'who diverges most' is one obvious query away, and the moment it is answered on a dashboard, agreement with the machine becomes an unstated performance expectation with no notice and no appeal. The signal that this has happened is not a metric - it is interview panels becoming harder to staff, with scheduling given as the reason.

features.name: Deterministic gates via Claude Code hooks

Quality gate lives in .githooks/pre-commit (black on staged, flake8 repo-wide, tests with graceful skip when Postgres is down), enabled by core.hooksPath. The portable gates no longer live in this repo: they ship as the django-guardrails plugin from the evalforms-team-marketplace marketplace, declared in the committed .claude/settings.json. Only three repo-specific hooks stayed in .claude/hooks/ (check-layout-drift.sh, reinject-context.sh, session-telemetry.py). PASS/FAIL matrix: /django-guardrails:hooks-matrix, 43 PASS expected.

features.name: template_form/services.py leaks the API layer
features.description: Found while scoping ARCH-3: template_form/services.py imports rest_framework.serializers and django.http.JsonResponse, and evaluation_form/services.py imports rest_framework.exceptions. A service returning an HTTP response cannot be reused off the request path (Celery task, management command). This is why guard-layering.py only enforces the broadcast rule - a no-DRF-in-services gate would be red on day one and get switched off. Clean these up first, then extend the hook.

features.name: Pre-commit gate cannot run tests locally
features.description: Found while building ARCH-3, then found to be worse than recorded. The original entry said .githooks/pre-commit skips the test stage when Postgres is unreachable, so a commit made with docker-compose down is lint-checked only. The truth: the test stage has never run at all. Its db_reachable probe launches the local interpreter and calls connection.ensure_connection(), but the local interpreter never loads .env - only docker-compose does - so the probe dies on ImproperlyConfigured: SECRET_KEY must not be empty, before it ever reaches the database. Confirmed by reproducing the probe by hand while evaluation_form_service-db-1 was Up 2 hours: the gate still printed 'Postgres недоступний' and advised docker-compose up -d db, which cannot help. So every commit in this repo has been lint-only, and the message named the wrong cause each time. Fixed on 2026-08-25: the runner is now whichever RUNNING compose service holds manage.py (found by probing, not by name), with the local interpreter as fallback; the probe's stderr is printed instead of discarded, so the message names the real cause; timeout is optional, since it ships with coreutils and its absence used to read as a dead database too. Two more defects surfaced in the same block and were fixed with it: the test invocation was `cmd | tail`, whose exit code comes from tail, so red tests would never have failed the gate even once the probe worked; and the probe's own output was going to /dev/null. Verified three ways - a live run now prints Ran 78 tests OK through docker compose exec, a PATH without docker prints the actual OperationalError, and the pipe change was demonstrated to catch a failure the old form swallowed. Still open: the sqlite-profile or ephemeral-Postgres idea, which only matters for machines with no compose running.

features.name: TemplateForm and WorkingForm paginate without an ordering
features.description: Surfaced as UnorderedObjectListWarning in a full test run (71/71 green, so nothing failed): DRF paginated both list endpoints over an unordered queryset, free to repeat or skip a row between ?page=1 and ?page=2. Fixed in two layers, because one was not enough. Model layer: TemplateForm.Meta (new), WorkingForm.Meta and EvaluationForm.Meta now carry a deterministic ordering with a -pk tiebreaker - created_at is auto_now_add and clone_template_to_working stamps a batch inside one transaction, so equal sort keys are the normal case. View layer: both list endpoints annotate with Count(), which adds a GROUP BY, and Django ignores Meta.ordering in grouped queries (QuerySet.ordered returns False) - so TemplateFormViewSet got an `ordering` default for its OrderingFilter and WorkingFormViewSet, which has no filter_backends, got an explicit .order_by() after the annotate. Three AlterModelOptions migrations, no schema change. Caught by a test asserting the endpoint emits no UnorderedObjectListWarning; the Meta-only fix passed the config assertions and still failed that one.

features.name: Nine more models paginate without an ordering
features.description: Found while closing BUG-6, deliberately left out of its scope. Only the three form models were fixed; a sweep over the pipeline apps shows these still have an empty Meta.ordering: TemplateFormTopic, TemplateFormItems, ReadOnlyFormTopic, WorkingFormTopic, WorkingFormItem, Candidate, EvaluationFormTopic, EvaluationFormItem, EvaluationScore, EvaluationFeedback. At least six of them are reachable through a paginated list route (the nested working-form topics/items, template-form items, and the candidates / evaluation-scores / evaluation-feedbacks routes), so they carry the same page-boundary defect. No test paginates them today, which is exactly why the suite stayed silent. The topic and item viewsets also use get_annotated_list(), so the GROUP BY trap from BUG-6 applies there too and a Meta.ordering alone will not be enough. Reference data (Question, Topic, TechStack, Project) is already ordered.

features.name: Published plugin still documents this repo's files as if they were universal
features.description: Found while moving django-guardrails to the marketplace (task 5b). Lives in the OTHER repo: AndriiRuhlyuk/evalforms-team-marketplace, at plugins/django-guardrails/skills/scaffold-tests/references/conventions.md. It cites concrete paths from this project - working_form/tests/tests_working_forms.py as the model test file, prefetch_count() from working_form/utils.py - as though every Django repo had them. In any other consumer repo those references are simply false, and a skill that cites a file the reader cannot open is worse than one that stays abstract. Deliberate at the time: the move was a 1:1 copy, not a refactor, and the risk of rewriting 23 files under a version bump outweighed the benefit while there is exactly one consumer. Fix before a second team installs the plugin: either generalise the guidance, or mark the examples as drawn from a reference implementation.

features.name: Marketplace version check leaks a Python literal into its message
features.description: Found while moving django-guardrails to the marketplace (task 5b). Lives in the OTHER repo: AndriiRuhlyuk/evalforms-team-marketplace, at scripts/check-versions.py. When plugin.json has no version key at all, the mismatch report prints "plugin.json has 'None'" - Python's None reaching a human-facing string through an f-string over a dict .get(). The check itself is correct and the CI job still fails as it should; only the message misleads, since a reader looks for a literal "None" in the JSON. Print "(missing)" for the absent-key case and keep quotes for real values.

features.name: Marketplace CI warns on a deprecated Node runtime
features.description: Found while moving django-guardrails to the marketplace (task 5b). Lives in the OTHER repo: AndriiRuhlyuk/evalforms-team-marketplace, at .github/workflows/validate-plugins.yml. Both jobs emit "Node.js 20 is deprecated" - it comes from actions/checkout@v4, not from any code we wrote, and nothing fails today. Recorded so the next reader does not re-investigate a green run: the fix is bumping the action, and it becomes real work only when GitHub drops the runtime.

features.name: Marketplace version check passes when no version exists anywhere
features.description: Found while fixing ARCH-7. Lives in the OTHER repo: AndriiRuhlyuk/evalforms-team-marketplace, at scripts/check-versions.py. The invariant is written as an inequality between two dict.get() calls, so when BOTH marketplace.json and plugin.json lack a version key the comparison is None != None, which is false, and CI goes green on a marketplace that declares no version at all. This is the exact failure the check exists to prevent, inverted: the version-sync invariant is the one thing the plan named as non-optional, and its blind spot is the case where there is nothing to sync. Fix by requiring the key to be present before comparing values.

features.name: Manifest validator misreports and crashes on a non-string version
features.description: Found while fixing ARCH-7. Lives in the OTHER repo: AndriiRuhlyuk/evalforms-team-marketplace, at scripts/validate.py. Two independent defects on the version field. Line 116 formats it as f"'{version!r}'" - !r already adds quotes, so the message prints ''1.0.0'' and a reader cannot tell whether the stray quotes are part of the value. The second defect was originally recorded as a TypeError from VERSION_RE.match() on a non-string, on the premise that version was the one required key missing from REQUIRED_PLUGIN_STRING_KEYS - that premise was false (it was added in a3124ab) and the report had been written against an older tree. The real defect at the same spot: the type check and the emptiness check shared one condition, so any wrong type was reported as "empty or whitespace-only" - a message that sends the reader looking for whitespace that is not there. Fixed by splitting them, which repairs the message for all five string keys rather than just version. Recorded as a correction because the wrong premise reached this registry before anyone re-read the file.

features.name: Published plugin's executable code assumes this repo's compose services
features.description: Found while fixing ARCH-6, and deliberately left out of its scope because ARCH-6 was a text fix. The prose in scaffold-tests no longer claims another repo's paths exist, but the scripts still do: scripts/preflight.py hardcodes REQUIRED_SERVICES = ("db", "celery") and probes the database through the celery container, so a consumer without compose or with different service names gets a blocked verdict at step 1 - there is a --no-docker escape but no flag for a different service name. scripts/verify-tests.sh carries the same docker-compose exec -T celery default in TEST_CMD, its --help and its coverage branch, though TEST_CMD is at least a documented override. Separately, SKILL.md's allowed-tools front matter permits Bash(.venv/bin/black:*) and Bash(.venv/bin/flake8:*) specifically, so a uv or poetry project gets a permission prompt on every lint call - widening that list is a security decision, not a text edit. Portability of the prose is done; portability of the code is not.

features.name: deny and hook ask are not interchangeable layers
features.description: Found while verifying the non-blocking gates after the marketplace move, then corrected by investigation - the first version of this entry had the mechanism backwards. The order is: the PreToolUse hook runs FIRST, and an exit-2 hook stops the call before permission rules are read at all. Anything else a hook returns is advice; deny and ask rules are evaluated afterwards, and a matching deny wins. So on a plain `git clean ...` the guard-migrations branch is not unreachable - it runs, builds its warning about unrecoverable untracked migrations, and changes nothing, because Bash(git clean *) under deny had already decided. Verified empirically: `git clean -n` returns the permission layer's wording, not the hook's Ukrainian text. Keep the overlap rather than removing it. deny matches by prefix, so `sudo git clean -fd` walks past it and the hook becomes the only guard. Of the ten trigger branches in this hook, five are covered by NO permission rule at all (rm/mv/shred on migration files, git checkout without --, git reset, git stash, find -delete) - there the hook is the only thing standing, which combined with ARCH-13 means they currently guard nothing. Never relax a deny entry on the theory that the hook covers it: what you get back is a prompt, not a block.

features.name: Destructive git forms slip past both the hook and the permission rules
features.description: Found while investigating ARCH-12, by feeding synthetic payloads to guard-migrations.sh directly. The hook lives in the OTHER repo now: AndriiRuhlyuk/evalforms-team-marketplace, at plugins/django-guardrails/hooks/guard-migrations.sh - patching the ~/.claude/plugins/cache copy is pointless, the next marketplace update overwrites it. Silent in BOTH layers, each confirmed: `git -C <path> clean -fd` (the hook's regex wants `git` immediately before `clean`, so any global flag breaks it, and deny matches by prefix so it misses too); `git reset --hard` and `git stash` with no literal word migrations in the command (those branches sit under a `case *migrations*` guard, and no permission rule covers them) - untracked migrations die quietly; `git checkout .`; `tee <file>`; `cp /dev/null <file>`; and a python -c calling shutil.rmtree. `>>` redirection is covered correctly. The `git -C` gap is the clearest one to fix and it is a defect of the portable hook, not of this repo's configuration. RESOLVED in django-guardrails 1.1.0. Every form listed above is now caught. The git prefix in all branches accepts git's global options by name (-C, -c, --git-dir=, --work-tree=, --namespace=, --exec-path=, --no-pager, --bare, -p, pathspec flags); a name list rather than "any tokens between git and clean", which would fire on `git commit -m "clean up"`. The tree-wide rollback forms (git reset --hard, git checkout ., git restore <path>, git stash -u) are now checked ABOVE the `case *migrations*` filter, since they destroy migrations without ever containing the word; git restore --staged is excluded and git checkout <branch> is left ungated on purpose. tee/cp/install and a python -c with shutil.rmtree/os.remove/Path().unlink are covered as block. Regression cases live in test-hooks.sh and were mutation-checked: reverting the git-option prefix makes the `git -C` case fail. Note found while doing that - the payload `--git-dir=/repo/.git clean` passes even with the broken regex, because the literal ".git clean" matches by accident; the test now uses a path without the .git suffix.

features.name: The whole ask layer is inert in an auto-approving session
features.description: Found while trying to prove guard-migrations.sh fires live. Running `rm working_form/migrations/0099_probe_nonexistent.py` produced no prompt at all - the command just ran. The hook is not at fault: fed the identical payload by hand it returns a correct permissionDecision "ask" with its explanation about breaking the migration dependency graph. The delivery is what fails. Confirmed from a second, independent direction: `docker-compose down --help`, which matches the `Bash(docker-compose down *)` entry under permissions.ask in .claude/settings.json, also ran with no prompt. So it is not a plugin defect and not a settings defect - in a session whose permission mode auto-approves, every ask-shaped guard is silently inert, whether it comes from settings or from a hook. Three explanations were ruled out rather than assumed. The rule is not missing: the /permissions panel lists Bash(docker-compose down *) under Ask, alongside the migrate and migrations-edit entries, under the promise that Claude Code will always ask. The pattern is not wrong: it matches the command that ran. The config is not overridden: defaultMode is default at project level and unset at local and user level, with no environment variable in play. What remains is the session's runtime permission mode, which is set interactively, is not written to any settings file, and therefore cannot be read back from one - the same shape of mistake this session kept finding, where the readable source is not the deciding one. What still works: deny rules (git push and .env stayed blocked all session) and exit-2 hooks (protect-secrets and guard-layering both blocked real writes). The consequence is that guard-migrations, the migration-editing ask rules, and the docker-compose down rule protect nothing in such a session while looking exactly like protection that is present. Decide deliberately: either run this repo in a mode where ask is honoured, or promote the guards that actually matter from ask to deny or exit 2. RESOLVED by the second option, in django-guardrails 1.1.0. The guard-migrations branches whose false-positive risk is near zero now exit 2 instead of asking: git clean in any form, and rm/mv/shred/truncate/dd, tee/cp/install, find -delete, output redirection and shutil.rmtree aimed at a path under migrations/. exit 2 runs before permission rules are read, so it holds in any session mode. The forms that are often legitimate (git reset --hard, git checkout ., git restore, git stash -u) stayed on ask deliberately: a false exit 2 cannot be waved through from the session, so the cost of over-blocking there is higher than the protection. Residual risk is tracked as ARCH-15.

features.name: The ask-shaped guards that were NOT promoted still protect nothing here
features.description: The remainder of ARCH-13 after the 1.1.0 fix. Three groups of guards are still delivered through the ask channel and are therefore inert in a session whose permission mode auto-approves: the four permissions.ask entries in .claude/settings.json (python manage.py migrate, docker-compose down, and the two Edit(**/migrations/**) patterns), and the guard-migrations branches left on ask on purpose (git reset --hard, git checkout ., git restore, git stash -u). Nothing about them is broken - they are correct rules delivered over a channel this repo's sessions do not honour, which is worse than an absent rule because /permissions displays them as active protection. Do not promote them reflexively: migrate under deny would block ordinary work, and exit 2 on git checkout . cannot be overridden from the session. The honest options are to run the repo in a mode that honours ask, or to accept them as documentation rather than enforcement. Verify before acting: the runtime permission mode is set interactively and is not readable from any settings file, so the only proof is to run one of these commands and see whether a prompt appears. RESOLVED in django-guardrails 1.2.0, by replacing rather than promoting. docker-compose down gave way to an exit-2 branch on the -v form specifically, which is the one that drops the volume and with it the django_migrations table; plain down still passes. The two Edit(**/migrations/**) patterns gave way to the new guard-migration-edits.py hook, which blocks an edit only when git already tracks the file - a committed migration is in colleagues' checkouts and applied somewhere, so changing it diverges schemas silently, while an uncommitted one is yours to edit, which is exactly what writing a data migration by hand needs. Both were then deleted from permissions.ask, leaving one entry there, manage.py migrate, kept deliberately as a reminder and documented in CLAUDE.md as nothing more. The four soft git forms in the plugin stay on ask by the same reasoning as in 1.1.0. The general lesson is in CLAUDE.md: before adding anything to ask, check whether the same question can be decided from the filesystem or from git.

features.name: Deleting the parent directory bypasses the migrations gate entirely
features.description: Noticed while fixing ARCH-14, not yet addressed. Every rm/mv/find branch in guard-migrations.sh sits under a `case *migrations*` filter, so it only sees commands that spell the word out. `rm -rf working_form/` destroys the app's migrations without containing it, and the same holds for `mv working_form /tmp/`, `rsync --delete` onto an app directory, and any script invoked by path (`python cleanup.py`) whose destructive work is invisible in the command text. The repo's own deny rule `Bash(rm -rf *)` covers the first form here but is prefix-matched, so `sudo rm -rf` and `cd app && rm -rf x` walk past it, and it does not travel with the plugin to other repos. A fix has to decide what counts as a Django app directory from the command text alone, which is why it was not folded into 1.1.0 - the false-positive surface is much wider than the migrations/ path check. Same class of limit, worth stating once: the hook reads the literal command, so an indirection it cannot expand (a shell variable, eval, a git alias) hides any of this from every branch. RESOLVED in django-guardrails 1.2.0. The directory case is decided from the filesystem instead of the text: every path token of an rm/mv/shred command (and rsync --delete) is resolved against CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR and checked with find -maxdepth 3 -type d -name migrations -quit, so `rm -rf working_form`, `rm -rf .` and `mv working_form /tmp/` all block while `rm -rf staticfiles` and a non-existent path stay silent. Of the indirection classes, two turned out to be decidable and were closed: git aliases are read from git config and re-scanned as `git <value>` (a separate pass rather than string substitution, so an alias named st cannot corrupt `git status`), and a script invoked by path is read from disk and scanned with the same patterns, with comment lines stripped and a 64 KB ceiling. The third class was already covered and had been mis-stated in the original note: `C="git clean -fd"; $C` contains the literal text `git clean` in the very same command, so the existing patterns see it. What genuinely remains is ARCH-17. All five additions were mutation-checked: removing each one makes exactly its own case fail, and removing the comment filter turns the negative case red rather than green.

features.name: What the migrations gate still cannot see, after 1.2.0
features.description: The honest remainder, recorded so nobody re-derives it. The hook decides from the command text plus three extra sources (filesystem, git aliases, contents of a script named by path), and each has an edge past it. Text assembled across calls: a variable set in one Bash invocation and used in the next, or built from fragments (C="git cl"; C="$C ean -fd"), or decoded at runtime (base64, eval of a computed string) - the deciding text never exists in any single command, so no pattern can match it. Script scanning stops at the first level: a scanned script that invokes another script hides the second one, and a heredoc or string literal inside a scanned script reads as code, which is a false-positive risk in the other direction. Files above 64 KB or outside CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR are not read at all. The filesystem check resolves plain tokens only, so a glob or a command substitution in the path is invisible, and it cannot see a path that does not exist yet. None of these is worth chasing: they describe deliberate circumvention rather than the accident the gate exists to prevent, and every additional layer of expansion widens the false-positive surface of a decision that cannot be overridden from the session. Revisit only if one of them shows up in a real incident.

features.name: Marketplace CI validated manifests but never ran the hook self-test matrices
features.description: Found while adding the second plugin. The plugin-validate job ran `claude plugin validate` and an optional smoke install - both prove the manifest is well formed, neither proves a gate still bites. Every plugin ships hooks/test-hooks.sh, and until now it ran only when a human typed the hooks-matrix command. A hook that quietly stopped blocking, or started blocking everything, would reach main with a green tick. Fixed in the same change: plugin-validate now runs hooks/test-hooks.sh for each plugin in the matrix that has one, guarded by a file test so a plugin without hooks does not fail the job. Costs nothing in CI - the matrix needs neither an API key nor the network, only python3 and jq. Verified on the first run after the push, not inferred from a green tick: run 32902048724 on marketplace commit 6b1925c logged `Разом: 53 PASS, 0 FAIL` under plugin-validate (drf-api-guard) and `Разом: 79 PASS, 0 FAIL` under plugin-validate (django-guardrails). That distinction matters because the step is guarded by `if [ -f "$suite" ]`, whose else branch prints `nothing to run` and exits 0 - a job that never found the matrix would still be green. Both totals present means both matrices actually executed.

features.name: drf-api-guard: three deliberate blind spots in the access gate
features.description: Recorded so nobody re-derives them. First, only module-level classes are checked: a factory function that builds and returns a ViewSet without permissions passes. Rejected on purpose - the pattern is rare and a false positive on a test fixture or a serializer factory costs more than the miss. Second, grandfathering keys on the class name, so renaming a legacy violator reads as introducing a new one and the gate demands permissions. Wrong in the safe direction, but still wrong. Third, rule 3 (writes from a serializer method that is not create/update/save) has no grandfathering at all: PostToolUse cannot see the before state, so a file carrying an old write in validate() warns on every edit. Tolerable only because that rule warns rather than blocks. Revisit the second one first if it bites. Fourth, adjacent rather than a blind spot: the `# noqa: api-guard` opt-out is broader than it reads. It silences both blocking rules, not just the permissions one, and it propagates to subclasses declared in the same file. Documented in the plugin README; recorded here because a reviewer skimming a diff for that comment needs to know it can be doing more than exempting the line it sits on.

features.name: Marketplace registration has five places, not three - and two were silently skipped on the previous release
features.description: Found while adding django-deploy-checklist. Both the orchestration plan and the marketplace README stated that a new plugin needs three places: the plugins/ directory, the marketplace.json entry, and the matrix.plugin list in the workflow. Measuring the repository showed two more that nothing checks. drf-api-guard, released before this change, was missing from BOTH: it had no row in .github/CODEOWNERS, so review of that plugin was never routed to its owner (the default `*` rule masks this - a reviewer is still assigned, so the state is indistinguishable from correct until there is more than one owner), and no row in the README plugin table, so a consumer reading the front page would not learn the plugin exists. Neither omission makes CI red, because both validators read only marketplace.json and plugin.json; the workflow list, CODEOWNERS and the README carry no machine-comparable structure to check against. Fixed here: both missing plugins added to both files, and the README section rewritten from three places to five with a table naming the consequence of each omission. One extra defect removed while there: the README plugin table carried a `Версія` column duplicating the version a third time, outside what scripts/check-versions.py compares - so it could drift silently and be believed. The column is gone and the README now states that marketplace.json is the single source.

features.name: django-deploy-checklist: four deliberate blind spots in the release checklist
features.description: Recorded so nobody re-derives them, and revised after an adversarial review that overturned one of the four. First and most dangerous, unchanged: an application-level wait in a dependent service downgrades compose-readiness from RED to YELLOW, but the script cannot prove the wait covers the service it was credited to. A command like `wait_for_db` is typically written for the database and does nothing for the message broker, so on this project redis - the one dependency with no wait of any kind - receives the same YELLOW as db, which is genuinely guarded. The finding text says so explicitly, but a reader skimming levels would read YELLOW as checked. Second, unchanged: env keys are collected only from settings.py and any .py inside a settings/ package; a read from a task or a management command is invisible. Widening it would pull in tests and scripts that read variables which must not exist in production. Third, RESOLVED: the original note said a task name built from the file path would report a live task as missing under a src/ layout, and the review reproduced exactly that. Names are now compared by dotted suffix rather than equality, and library namespaces (celery., django_celery_beat., django_celery_results.) are always treated as declared, so celery.backend_cleanup in a fixture no longer blocks. The residue is a deliberate trade: a task whose suffix happens to collide with another is missed. For a RED-level rule a miss is cheaper than a false blocker. Fourth, unchanged: migration-hygiene compares the working tree against HEAD, not history against history, so a migration that was edited AND committed in a separate commit is invisible - which is the common case in someone else's pull request, exactly where it matters most.

features.name: Environment sample declares 7 of the 11 keys the code actually reads
features.description: Measured, not inferred: settings.py reads 11 distinct environment keys, the sample declares 7. Four are read WITHOUT a default and are absent from the sample - CELERY_BROKER_URL, CELERY_RESULT_BACKEND, PEOPLEFORCE_API_KEY, PEOPLEFORCE_API_URL - so an environment assembled from the sample gets None for all four. Celery silently loses its broker, and the CRM integration sends requests with no key rather than failing loudly. A fifth, DJANGO_DEBUG, is absent but has a default of "False", which is the safe direction and only means nobody sets it deliberately. Nothing in the repository catches this: the sample is not compared to the code anywhere, and the deny rule Read(**/.env.*) means a session cannot casually diff them either. Reproduce with `python3 plugins/django-deploy-checklist/scripts/deploy-audit.py --repo .` from the marketplace clone - it reports exactly these four as RED and DJANGO_DEBUG as YELLOW. Fix is a one-line-per-key addition to the sample with placeholder values, never real ones.

features.name: manage.py check --deploy cannot run without a database, so the security warnings it exists to surface are never seen
features.description: Measured while designing the deploy checklist. Running `manage.py check --deploy` with dummy credentials fails with SystemCheckError, and the cause has nothing to do with deployment: drf_spectacular.E001 fires because schema generation opens a database connection, and a failed connection is reported as a check ERROR. The command therefore exits non-zero for a connectivity reason, which trains the reader to ignore its exit code. Underneath, when the connection does succeed, there are five genuine findings - security.W004 (no SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS), W008 (SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT not True), W012 (SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE not True), W016 (CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE not True), and W009 which only appeared because the probe used a dummy SECRET_KEY. They sit under eight lines of drf_spectacular W001/W002 noise about unresolved type hints. Two separate things to decide: whether to set the four security settings (they are production concerns and DEBUG is env-driven, so they are not automatic), and whether to silence the spectacular noise via SPECTACULAR_SETTINGS so the deploy check becomes readable at all. The /deploy-check command documents the trap in the meantime.

features.name: A self-test matrix only catches what its fixtures were written to expose - measured, not argued
features.description: The strongest evidence yet for how a green matrix misleads, and worth keeping because it cost nothing to find and would have cost a release to discover. django-deploy-checklist shipped its first version at 47 PASS, 0 FAIL, including a parity category specifically built to prove that its two docker-compose parsing branches agree. An adversarial subagent, told to build fixtures and run them rather than read and reason, found twelve defects that all 47 cases missed. Five shared one root: every fixture in the matrix was written WITHOUT comments, and the simplified parser stripped `#` nowhere. So `- store  # база` became a service name carrying its own comment, the dependency vanished, and a compose file with a real start-order race was reported clean. `condition: service_healthy  # чекаємо` stopped matching the constant and the healthiest possible file was reported sick. A wait token mentioned in a comment - `# TODO wait_for_db колись` - counted as a real wait and removed a release blocker. Parity could not catch any of it: parity compares two branches on the inputs it is given, and no given input let the bug appear. Four more were false release blockers reachable from ordinary use: `git diff --name-only HEAD` lists ADDED files too, so a plain `git add` on a fresh migration produced RED 'already applied elsewhere' about a file that was never in history. The general lesson, stated once: a matrix measures the author's imagination, and the cheapest way to widen it is to hand the artefact to something that is trying to break it, with the rule that no claim counts without a fixture and a run. All twelve now have cases; the matrix is at 74 PASS, 0 FAIL. Second wave, worth recording separately because it is the failure mode of fixing: the comment-stripping fix introduced its own silent lie. Tracking quotes character by character meant an apostrophe inside an unquoted word - `command: echo don't panic  # TODO wait_for_db` - opened a quote state that never closed on that line, so the `#` counted as quoted, the comment stayed in the command text, and the wait-token defect came back from the dead. The re-check that found it was the same subagent, re-run against its OWN saved fixtures rather than new ones - which is the point: a fix is not verified by the tests written for it, only by the tests that caught the original. The rule is now YAML's own: a quote opens a scalar only where the scalar begins. Matrix at 82 PASS, 0 FAIL.

features.name: Marketplace CI runs the self-test matrices but reads only their exit code, so anything they say on stderr is invisible
features.description: The complement to ARCH-18, found by running a matrix rather than reading it. ARCH-18 made plugin-validate execute each plugin's matrix instead of merely validating its manifest; this is the half that fix did not cover. The job asserts on the exit code alone, and a matrix can be noisy, broken in its setup, or partially skipped while still exiting 0. Concretely: django-deploy-checklist 1.0.0 built its adv_bom fixture with `printf '\xef\xbb\xbf' >"$F/adv_bom/docker-compose.yaml.tmp" 2>/dev/null || mkdir -p "$F/adv_bom"` - an idiom that reads as 'write, and create the directory if that fails'. The 2>/dev/null silences nothing, because when a `>` redirection cannot open its file the message is printed by bash itself while expanding redirections left to right, before the second `2>` is in effect. So every run printed `No such file or directory` to stderr, the `||` branch then succeeded, the script exited 0, and CI was green over a matrix that was visibly complaining. Fixed in 1.0.1 for this one fixture (explicit mkdir -p before printf, trailing rm -f of the temp file dropped) and verified with stdout and stderr captured separately: 82 PASS, 0 FAIL, zero lines on stderr, run out of ~/.claude/plugins/cache/.../1.0.1/ rather than the worktree. The class stays open, which is why this entry is false: nothing anywhere compares a matrix's stderr against the empty string, so the next such workaround reaches main green in exactly the same way. The fix considered and deliberately deferred was to wrap fixture construction in a function, redirect its stderr to a file, and fail the run if that file is non-empty - roughly 800 lines of fixture setup to restructure, which is why it was scoped out rather than rejected. Same shape as ARCH-18's own lesson and ARCH-22's: a green tick proves the assertion that was written, never the one that was not.

features.name: The marketplace repository has no CLAUDE.md and no rules, so every gate is edited with zero repo-specific instruction loaded
features.description: Found while trimming this repo's CLAUDE.md from 255 lines to 166 and moving the plugin prose out. This repository carries CLAUDE.md plus fifteen path-scoped rules; AndriiRuhlyuk/evalforms-team-marketplace, which holds the source of every gate that fires here, carries none - its root has .claude-plugin/, .github/, plugins/, scripts/, README.md, CHANGELOG.md, SECURITY.md, and no .claude/ directory and no CLAUDE.md at all. The asymmetry hides itself: the session that changes a gate almost always starts in this repo, where the instructions do load, and only notices the gap when someone opens the marketplace worktree directly - at which point editing guard-migrations.sh, a file whose every branch is a deliberate decision, happens with nothing loaded to say why those branches exist. The new infra/gates.md here does not close it, because a rule is scoped by paths within its own repository and cannot reach across into another checkout. What belongs on that side and exists nowhere today: how hooks.json wires ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, why the gates are deliberately fail-open (a gate that blocks everything gets removed wholesale, leaving no protection at all), how to run each matrix locally out of the cache version directory rather than the worktree, and the release cycle in the maintainer's direction. Deliberately deferred rather than rejected: it is a separate repository with its own structure, and writing it from inside this one would produce a description of the plugins rather than of the code that implements them.

features.name: Nothing reconciles the plugin list in CLAUDE.md with enabledPlugins in settings.json, so the fourth plugin will make the file lie
features.description: Identified while writing the Gates and Plugins section that replaced 106 lines of plugin prose. CLAUDE.md now names three plugins in prose; .claude/settings.json declares the same three under enabledPlugins, and that declaration is the one that actually matters, since it is what the CLI reads. Nothing compares them. Adding a fourth plugin necessarily edits settings.json - the plugin does not load otherwise - and leaves CLAUDE.md silently stale, which is worse than an omitted line, because the file is read as authoritative and a reader has no way to tell a complete list from an outdated one. This is the same class as two findings already recorded: the version numbers deleted from CLAUDE.md in this same session, on the stated grounds that a number copied into the file is a place to drift that nothing checks, and ARCH-20's README plugin table, which carried a duplicated version column for exactly this reason. The fix is cheap and every piece of machinery already exists: check-layout-drift.sh already parses CLAUDE.md, already emits a divergence into context via jq, and jq is already a hard dependency of that hook - `jq -r '.enabledPlugins|keys[]' .claude/settings.json` yields the authoritative names, each of which should appear somewhere in the file, and a name in the file that is not in enabledPlugins is the mirror error worth reporting too. Left open on purpose in this session, to keep the documentation change and the hook change separately revertable.

features.name: Hypothesis: reading a rule file with Read appears to consume its automatic injection, delivering only what was read
features.description: One observation, recorded because it changes how the rule system can be verified at all, not because it is established - and explicitly marked as unreproduced. In session 3bf2d6e4, opening topic/models.py loaded workflow.md and data/models.md but not general.md, whose glob **/*.py matches and which had fired on every comparable trigger in the history of .claude/instructions.log, including .claude/hooks/guard-layering.py and .claude/skills/scaffold-tests/scripts/mutate.py. The one difference in that turn: .claude/rules/general.md had been opened with Read in the same message. Proposed mechanism: the harness treats a rule already present in context as loaded and does not re-inject it, so reading the file as text consumes the injection while delivering only the portion actually read - six lines of frontmatter, in that instance, instead of the fifty-two-line rule. If true, the consequence is sharp: any attempt to inspect a rule by reading it destroys the thing being inspected, and .claude/instructions.log becomes the only non-destructive way to ask what loaded. To confirm or kill it: one fresh session that opens a .py without touching any rule file, confirming general.md in the log; then a second fresh session that reads general.md first and opens the same .py; compare. Worth pairing with the other error from the same session, where gates.md was declared a dead rule on the evidence of a session whose rule index predated the file's existence - later refuted by a clean run in session 0f2129cb, which logged gates.md loading with trigger .claude/settings.json and globs normalised to .claude/settings.json, .claude/hooks, .githooks, .claude/rules. Both mistakes share one shape: a conclusion drawn from a single session without checking what that session could have known.

features.name: No release boundary exists anywhere: zero git tags, no CHANGELOG.md, and the documented commit prefixes cover fewer than half the commits
features.description: Measured while scoping an SDK automation script, and recorded because three separate gaps are entangled and only the first is obvious. First, `git tag` returns nothing: 90 commits, zero tags, so no marker anywhere says which commit was a release. Second, `find . -iname 'CHANGELOG*'` matches no file: nothing in the repository states what shipped when. This is not a lapse in following a convention - README.md's Git Workflow section (lines 158-173) documents branches, commit prefixes and the PR flow but never a versioning or tagging step, so the convention was never written down to be broken. Third, and the one that actually bites automation: README line 170 documents four commit prefixes (Add:, Fix:, Update:, Remove:), while the history uses seven - Add: 13, Docs: 9, Fix: 7, Update: 6, Chore: 3, Refactor: 2, Remove: 1 - and the remaining 49 of 90 commits carry no recognizable prefix at all. Any generator that categorizes by conventional-commit prefix would therefore silently drop more than half the history and would have no mapping for Docs:, Chore: or Refactor:, the three prefixes in active use that the documented set omits. The concrete consequence measured today: the release-notes pipeline the 5.7 course demo is built around - `git log <tag>..HEAD` between two tags, patched into docs/CHANGELOG.md - cannot run against this repository at all; its pre-check exits before the agent is ever invoked. A date-bounded substitute (--since) runs but answers a different question, because a week is not a release. Deliberately deferred rather than rejected, and the three parts are separable and differently priced: adopting Keep a Changelog (https://keepachangelog.com/) is one file plus a habit; tagging retroactively requires deciding which of the 90 commits were releases, which nobody currently knows and which cannot be recovered from the history; reconciling the prefix list is a choice between widening README's four to the seven in use and accepting the drift as untracked. One correction worth keeping so it is not re-derived: the link supplied when this was raised, https://changelog.md/, is a commercial SaaS for feedback collection and hosted release-note publishing, not the file convention - it solves a different problem and would leave the repository with neither a tag nor a tracked file.

features.name: check-layout-drift.sh splits directory names on whitespace, so one real directory is reported as two that do not exist
features.description: Measured 2026-08-29 while merging the sync_features branch. The hook collects top-level directories with `for d in $(find . -maxdepth 1 -type d ...)` at lines 121 and 129, and unquoted command substitution is split on IFS before the loop ever sees a value. The repository has one directory named `5.7-sdk копія/` (lecture material for module 5.7), and the hook therefore reports two paths, `5.7-sdk/` and `копія/`, neither of which exists. Both are then presented as drift that must be reconciled into the ## Project Layout tree in CLAUDE.md, so obeying the hook literally would write two fabricated directories into the one file the project treats as authoritative about its own structure. The same script already knows the correct idiom: lines 61 and 111 read their input with `while IFS= read -r`, so this is an inconsistency inside a single file rather than an unknown technique. Note also that .gitignore cannot silence it - the entry `/5.7-sdk*` added on this branch keeps the directory out of git, but the hook walks the filesystem, not the index, so the phantom pair survives every ignore rule. Fix: `find ... -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d ''`, or at minimum the `while IFS= read -r` form already used twice above. Left open deliberately: the merge itself was the priority, and the hook change should be separately revertable. Note for anyone reproducing this: the directory that triggered it, `5.7-sdk копія/`, was deleted on the same day the finding was recorded, so the hook is currently silent and the defect is dormant, not fixed. To reproduce, create any top-level directory whose name contains a space and run the hook: it will report one path per whitespace-separated word. The .gitignore entry `/5.7-sdk*` was deliberately left in place for the same directory, since the lecture material can be downloaded again and the entry carries a comment explaining why the leading slash matters.

features.name: guard-migrations.sh fires on commands that delete nothing, and the message names a destruction that is not in the command
features.description: Two measured false positives, recorded together because the shape is the same and a gate that bites without cause teaches people to route around it. First, observed 2026-08-28: a single `git add` naming several files at once is blocked, while adding the same files one at a time, or `git add -u`, passes - the workaround is real but it is a workaround, not a fix. Second, measured 2026-08-29: a read-only bash loop (`for c in $(git rev-list ...)` with `git rev-parse "$c:$f"` inside, used to check whether an untracked file matched some commit's blob) was refused with the text 'Під шляхом . лежать файли міграцій, і команда знищує його цілком', attributing the trigger to a line in tools/sync_features/tests/test_guard.py. The command contained no rm, no clean, no checkout and no reset, and wrote nothing at all. The cost is not the interruption: it is that the refusal text asserts a specific destructive effect, so a reader who trusts it will believe a harmless command was dangerous, and a reader who learns not to trust it will stop reading the same message when it is correct. Worth pairing with the plugin's own hooks-matrix, which is the existing mechanism for proving a gate still bites: the matrix should gain a negative row per false positive above, so a fix is verified against both directions rather than only against real deletions. Two further triggers on 2026-08-29, and together they identify the mechanism, which the first two only hinted at. The third: a single shell line that created a throwaway file, linted it, discarded it, and then changed directory into the worktree was refused on the grounds that the worktree directory itself was being destroyed - the discard named a different file entirely. The fourth is the decisive one: invoking a Python script by path was refused with the reason line naming that script as the source, and the script contained no destructive call at all, only prose describing this very finding. So the hook resolves file paths mentioned anywhere in the command, reads those files, and matches destructive patterns against their contents rather than against the command being run. That single mechanism explains all four cases, including the first: a multi-file staging command hands it several files to read. It also means the hook cannot be reasoned about from the command line alone, which is why the refusal text feels arbitrary at the moment it fires. The workaround stayed the same throughout - one command per call, and wording that avoids quoting a destructive command verbatim - which is exactly the habit that erodes a gate: four refusals in one session, none of them real, each worked around rather than investigated. Any fix should be validated by the plugin's own hooks-matrix, extended with a negative row per case above, so that both directions are proven.

features.name: flake8 per-file-ignores is path-exact, so any git worktree inside the repository makes the clean baseline turn red on a file nobody touched
features.description: Measured 2026-08-29, immediately after merging a branch developed in .claude/worktrees/. Running `.venv/bin/flake8` from the repository root reported two E402 findings in .claude/worktrees/sdk-sync-features/evaluation_form_service/asgi.py; the same run with `--extend-exclude=.claude/worktrees` reported zero. Cause: setup.cfg line 25 grants the E402 exemption to the exact path `evaluation_form_service/asgi.py` - the exemption Channels genuinely requires, since get_asgi_application() must run before app modules import - and the worktree copy of that same file sits at a different path, so the exemption does not apply to it. The `exclude` list (setup.cfg lines 13-19) covers .git, .venv, __pycache__, migrations, staticfiles and media, but not .claude/worktrees. This matters more than the two lines suggest, because both CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules/general.md state that flake8 must exit clean and that any output at all is a regression introduced by the current diff. That rule is the only regression signal this repository has, and here it goes false-red for a file the diff never touched, purely because a worktree exists - which is exactly when someone is most likely to be checking whether their branch broke something. Fix: add `.claude/worktrees` to `exclude` in setup.cfg. The pre-commit gate runs flake8 through the same config, so the fix covers both paths. Fixed the same day, and the fix was forced rather than chosen: the pre-commit gate refused the very commit that recorded this finding, reporting the two phantom E402 and 'baseline цього репо - нуль'. The gate was right by its own rule; the configuration was what lied. Added `.claude/worktrees` to `exclude` in setup.cfg, with a comment stating why a worktree lints itself from its own root and the outer tree has no business linting a copy. Verified in both directions: `.venv/bin/flake8` with no flags now exits 0, and a deliberately broken file placed at the repository root still produced F401, F401 and E225, so the gate did not go blind in exchange.

features.name: flake8 keeps an ignore list of its own, so the gitignored sdlc/ toolkit was linted and one finding inside it blocked every commit in the repository
features.description: Measured 2026-09-01, when the pre-commit gate refused a commit made of two .md files and no Python at all. black reported 'пропущено, .py у staged немає', flake8 reported exactly one finding - F401 'os' imported but unused at sdlc/scripts/sdlc_lint.py:13 - and the gate closed with 'PRE-COMMIT FAILED: flake8: 1 знахідок / baseline цього репо - нуль'. The gate was right by its own rule; the configuration was what lied, the same way it did in CFG-3. Cause: sdlc/ is a vendored third-party toolkit (MIT, genkovich/agentic-engineering-course), gitignored whole at .gitignore line 390, so git never shows it and it reads as absent. flake8 does not read .gitignore and never has - it keeps a separate exclude list in setup.cfg, which named .git, .venv, .claude/worktrees, __pycache__, migrations, staticfiles, media and reports, but not sdlc. A directory the repository deliberately does not track was therefore linted as if it were project code, and a finding in code nobody here maintains held the whole repository hostage: while the baseline is red no commit passes, including commits carrying no Python. Same failure shape as CFG-3, second directory, and the generalisation is worth stating once rather than rediscovering a third time - gitignored is not flake8-ignored, and every such directory has to be named in setup.cfg by hand. Fix: added sdlc to exclude in setup.cfg with a comment recording why, committed separately in 445d485 and committed first, because a red baseline blocks the very commit that would repair it. Verified in both directions rather than by the clean run alone, since a checker that has only ever reported zero proves nothing - the trap QA-8 recorded. Forward: a deliberately broken file placed at the repository root still produced F401, and the repo-wide run reported exactly one finding, that file, so the gate did not go blind in exchange for the exemption. Backward: the identical file placed inside sdlc/ never appeared in the repo-wide run. One nuance surfaced while verifying and is worth keeping: naming a path inside sdlc/ explicitly on the command line still lints it, because exclude filters the tree walk and not explicit arguments. The pre-commit gate invokes flake8 with no arguments, so the gate itself is covered, but a manual flake8 sdlc/<file> will still report findings, and that is not a regression.

features.name: A sync_features test hard-coded the worktree it was measured in, so the suite was green there and red everywhere else
features.description: Found and fixed 2026-08-29, during the post-merge verification of tools/sync_features. The suite ran 227 tests green inside .claude/worktrees/sdk-sync-features and 226 of 227 in the main checkout: test_probe_sandbox.test_real_measured_pair_read_absolute_vs_relative_path embedded the literal string '/Users/.../.claude/worktrees/sdk-sync-features/.env' as the journal half of a real measured pair. The function under test, probe_sandbox._journal_denied, resolves journal entries with guard._normalised against guard.REPO_ROOT, so under any other root that path normalises to '.claude/worktrees/.../.env', which does not equal the target '.env', and the assertion flipped to False. The product behaviour was correct throughout - a denial recorded for a path in some other tree must not count as a denial of the target - so this was the test encoding its environment, not the code being wrong. Fix: build the absolute half from guard.REPO_ROOT, keeping the property actually under test (stream carries the relative path the agent passed, journal carries the absolute path the CLI resolved before calling the hook) and dropping the accidental one. Verified the test still bites rather than merely passing: a journal entry from a foreign root yields False, and an ALLOW entry at the correct root yields False. Recorded because the class recurred four times in this one piece of work - a proof that silently depends on the environment it was captured in is worth less than no proof, since it reads as evidence right up to the moment it is moved.

features.name: Ten of sixteen file:line references in .claude/rules point at the wrong line, and nothing checks them
features.description: Measured 2026-09-01 by resolving every `path:line` reference in .claude/rules/data/models.md and .claude/rules/domain/forms-lifecycle.md against the symbol each one names. Sixteen references, ten wrong. Five miss by exactly one line and are harmless in practice - template_form/services.py 214 resolves to 213 (populate_snapshot_from_question), 729 to 728 (clone_template_to_working), 627 to 626 (save_template_draft), 653 to 652 (publish_template_form), working_form/services.py 484 to 485 (clone_working_from_working) - the eye still lands inside the named function. Five are far enough off to mislead: template_form/models.py 10 resolves to 31 (BaseForm), 177 to 258 (BaseFormItems), 148 to 223 (draft_data), 154 to 229 (has_unpublished_changes), and working_form/models.py 172 to 152 (WorkingForm.is_fully_approved). Following BaseFormItems:177 lands in the middle of TemplateForm, and is_fully_approved:172 lands in _build_base_name - both are real code that reads as though it were the cited symbol, which is worse than a line that simply does not exist. The drift has a direction and therefore a cause: every template_form/models.py reference is shifted forward, consistent with the soft-delete block (is_deleted / deleted_at / deleted_by plus both managers) having been inserted above them, while working_form/models.py shifted backward. The six that still hit - working_form/services.py 342, 177 and 254, working_form/utils.py:51, question/models.py:18, employee/models.py:5 - are correct because those files happened not to move, not because any mechanism keeps them correct. The cost is specific to where these live: .claude/rules is the automatic instruction layer, injected by path without anyone asking for it, so a wrong coordinate is consumed silently by every session that opens a matching file, and it is consumed as authoritative. CLAUDE.md opens by stating that if a line there contradicts the code the code wins and the line must be fixed, but nothing enforces that for the rules directory. Two fix directions, and they are not equivalent. Drop line numbers from the rules and anchor by symbol name only: needs no maintenance, because a rename appears in the diff while a line shift never does. Or keep the coordinates and add a .githooks checker that, for each `path.py:N` reference under .claude/rules, asserts line N of that file contains the named symbol; check-layout-drift.sh is the existing precedent for a doc-versus-code checker here, so the shape is already in the repo. Whichever is chosen, verify in both directions: a deliberately corrupted reference must fail the check and every corrected one must pass, because a checker that has only ever reported zero proves nothing - the same trap QA-8 recorded.

features.name: EvaluationScore and EvaluationFeedback __str__ read interviewer.username, a field Employee removes, so both render the literal 'None'
features.description: Measured 2026-09-01 while reading the evaluation models to build a domain glossary. evaluation_form/models.py:352 (EvaluationScore.__str__) and evaluation_form/models.py:417 (EvaluationFeedback.__str__) interpolate self.interviewer.username. Employee sets `username = None` at employee/models.py:81 so that email can be the USERNAME_FIELD; Django drops the field from the model and leaves a plain class attribute holding None, so the expression does not raise - it renders the four characters 'None'. That is the worst of both outcomes: no exception to notice it, and no interviewer identity where the string is actually read. It is read in the Django admin change lists and the nested_admin inlines for both models, in DRF default error messages when the unique_together constraint names the instance, and in any log line that stringifies a score or a feedback - precisely the places someone looks to find out which interviewer scored what. A grep over the repository excluding migrations and .venv returns these two lines and nothing else, so the blast radius is exactly two __str__ methods and no behaviour changes with the fix. Employee already exposes what is needed: a `fullname` property built from first_name and last_name, and an __str__ that returns it, so interpolating the interviewer object itself is the minimal change. One caveat against reaching for fullname unguarded: neither name field is required by the model, so an employee created without them yields a single space - worse than 'None' for debugging, because it is invisible in a log. email is the only always-populated identifier (unique and required as USERNAME_FIELD), so the version that never degrades falls back to it. Verify by asserting the interviewer segment of each __str__ for a fully populated Employee and for one with both name fields blank; asserting merely that the output does not contain the substring 'None' is not sufficient, because EvaluationScore.score is legitimately nullable and that branch prints 'Not scored'.
